name: 4Ps of Marketing (Marketing Mix)
description: The classic checklist for turning a positioning into an executable marketing plan - Product, Price, Place, Promotion.
example: Prompt: "Plan the marketing mix for a new budget airline route." Product = no-frills economy seating; Price = below legacy-carrier fares; Place = direct app booking + budget travel aggregators; Promotion = social-first launch campaign targeting price-sensitive travelers.
steps: Product — what exactly are you selling, and which features matter to the target segment?
Price — what pricing model and level fits the segment's willingness-to-pay and the competitive set?
Place — which channels/locations should this be available through?
Promotion — how will the target segment actually hear about it, and what is the core message?
when_to_use: Use it once STP has defined who you are targeting and how, to structure the actual execution plan.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it as your opening structure for a "should we enter this market" case - it is an execution checklist, not a strategic decision framework.
pitfalls: Listing all four Ps generically without tying each back to the specific target segment's needs.
Treating Price as "as high as possible" instead of what the segment's willingness-to-pay and the competitive set actually support.

name: AIDA Funnel
description: A simple model of the stages a customer moves through before buying - Attention, Interest, Desire, Action - used to diagnose or design a marketing funnel.
example: A performance-marketing funnel: Attention = a scroll-stopping video ad; Interest = a landing page explaining the product; Desire = social proof and a limited-time offer; Action = a one-tap checkout.
steps: Attention — get noticed in a crowded environment (ads, PR, social reach).
Interest — hold their attention with relevant information once you have it.
Desire — build an emotional or rational reason to want this specifically.
Action — remove friction from the final step that converts interest into a purchase.
when_to_use: Use it for "how would you design this campaign" or "where in the funnel are we losing customers" questions.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it for post-purchase questions (retention, repeat usage) - AIDA stops at the first purchase; use AARRR/AARM instead for the fuller lifecycle.
pitfalls: Designing all four stages with the same message - each stage needs a different kind of content (Attention needs reach, Action needs a clear, low-friction next step).
Ignoring which stage is actually the bottleneck before proposing fixes across the whole funnel.

name: Ansoff Matrix
description: Maps four growth strategies along two axes - new vs. existing products, and new vs. existing markets - to structure "how should we grow" questions.
example: Prompt: "How should Zomato grow next?" Market Penetration = more orders from existing cities; Product Development = launch grocery delivery to existing users; Market Development = launch food delivery in a new country; Diversification = enter an unrelated business like fintech.
steps: X-axis: Products (Existing to New, left to right).
Y-axis: Markets (Existing to New, top to bottom).
Market Penetration (existing product, existing market): sell more of what you have to who you already serve - lowest risk.
Product Development (new product, existing market): new offerings for your current customers.
Market Development (existing product, new market): take what you have into a new segment/geography.
Diversification (new product, new market): highest risk, needs the strongest justification.
when_to_use: Use it for growth-strategy and scaling questions - "how should this company grow next", "should we launch this in a new market or a new product line".
when_not_to_use: Do not use it for a pure profitability/cost question, or when the growth options on the table do not actually differ by product/market newness.
pitfalls: Picking "Diversification" by default because it sounds ambitious - it is the highest-risk quadrant and needs strong justification, not enthusiasm.
Not being specific about what "new" means for this client - new to the company, or new to the world?

name: BCG Growth-Share Matrix
description: Classifies a company's products or business units on relative market share vs. market growth rate, to decide where to invest, hold, or divest.
example: Netflix's DVD-by-mail business became a "Cash Cow" (high share, low growth) that funded its "Star" streaming business (high share, high growth) during the transition.
steps: X-axis: Relative market share (High to Low, left to right).
Y-axis: Market growth rate (High to Low, top to bottom).
Stars (high share, high growth): invest to maintain leadership.
Question Marks (low share, high growth): invest selectively or divest - decide based on potential to become a Star.
Cash Cows (high share, low growth): harvest cash, invest minimally.
Dogs (low share, low growth): divest or hold only if strategically necessary.
when_to_use: Use it for portfolio-strategy questions - "which of these products should we invest in", "how should we allocate budget across this portfolio".
when_not_to_use: Do not use it for a single-product question (it needs a portfolio to compare) or when data on relative market share genuinely is not available.
pitfalls: Treating "Dogs" as automatically-kill - some Dogs are cash-neutral and strategically necessary (e.g. completing a product line).
Confusing market growth rate with market share - the two axes are easy to swap by mistake.

name: CAC vs LTV Unit Economics
description: The core unit economics engine comparing Customer Lifetime Value (LTV) against Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) to test business model sustainability.
example: B2B SaaS with $200/mo ARPU, 80% gross margin, and 2% monthly churn. LTV = ($200 × 0.80) / 0.02 = $8,000. If blended CAC is $2,000, LTV:CAC is 4.0x with a payback period of $2,000 / $160 = 12.5 months.
steps: Calculate Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) = Total Sales & Marketing Spend / Number of New Customers Acquired in period.
Calculate Customer Lifetime Value (LTV) = (Average Revenue Per User × Gross Margin %) / Churn Rate.
Evaluate the LTV:CAC Ratio: Healthy SaaS/Tech target is > 3.0x (3:1 to 5:1).
Calculate CAC Payback Period = CAC / (Monthly ARPU × Gross Margin %) (target is typically < 12 months for B2B, < 6 months for B2C).
Strategic Levers: To improve ratio, either reduce CAC (organic referrals, conversion optimization) or increase LTV (reduce churn, upsell/cross-sell, price increase).
when_to_use: Use when evaluating marketing channel ROI, unit economics, growth runway, and venture pitch readiness.
when_not_to_use: Do not calculate blended CAC when scaling paid marketing; look at marginal/paid CAC per specific acquisition channel.
pitfalls: Understating CAC by omitting sales team salaries, software overhead, or onboarding support costs.
Assuming zero customer churn over multiple years.
Calculating LTV on gross revenue instead of gross profit margin.

name: GTM Strategy Canvas
description: A one-page structure for planning a product or market launch - who you are targeting, what you are offering them, and how you will reach and convert them.
example: Prompt: "Plan the GTM for a new UPI-based lending product." Target segment: gig workers with thin credit files; value prop: instant approval using UPI transaction history; channels: partnerships with gig platforms, not broad ads; launch sequence: 1 city pilot, then scale by city.
steps: Target segment — who exactly is the first customer, and why them first?
Value proposition — what specific problem does this solve for that segment, in their words?
Channels — where does this segment actually spend attention, and which channels are cost-effective to reach them?
Pricing & offer — what is the launch offer, and does it match the segment's willingness-to-pay?
Sequencing — what is the phased rollout (one city/segment/channel first), and what triggers expansion to the next phase?
when_to_use: Use it for "how would you launch this product" or "plan the go-to-market for X" questions - broader than AIDA, covering strategy as well as funnel execution.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it for a pure positioning question with no launch/rollout component - use STP alone for that.
pitfalls: Writing a GTM plan with no sequencing - a real GTM plan phases what happens first (e.g. one city, one segment) before scaling.
Picking channels because they are trendy rather than because the target segment is actually there.

name: Product Life Cycle
description: Describes how a product's sales and competitive dynamics typically evolve through four stages - Introduction, Growth, Maturity, Decline - and what strategy fits each.
example: A legacy SaaS product past its growth peak, facing new competitors and slowing renewals, is likely in Maturity, not Decline - the right move is often defending share and extending the cycle, not writing it off.
steps: Introduction — low sales, high marketing spend, focus on awareness and early adopters.
Growth — sales accelerate, competitors enter, focus shifts to differentiation and distribution.
Maturity — growth slows, market is saturated, focus shifts to efficiency, retention, and defending share.
Decline — sales fall, focus shifts to harvesting cash, cost-cutting, or a deliberate exit/relaunch.
when_to_use: Use it to explain why a strategy that worked at launch should change later, or to diagnose which stage a declining product is in before recommending a fix.
when_not_to_use: Do not force-fit it onto a product whose trajectory genuinely does not follow this curve (e.g. a fad, or a product with structurally recurring demand) - state that explicitly rather than shoehorning it in.
pitfalls: Assuming every declining product is in "Decline" - a Maturity-stage dip from a fixable execution issue looks similar but needs a different fix.
Recommending the same playbook (aggressive growth spending) regardless of which stage the product is actually in.

name: STP (Segmentation, Targeting, Positioning)
description: The standard three-step process for deciding who to sell to and how to be seen by them, before any campaign or product decision.
example: Prompt: "How should a new D2C protein brand position itself against Whey Gold Standard?" Segment by fitness goal (not just age), target the "convenience-first" gym-goer segment, position as "the protein you will actually finish before it expires".
steps: Segmentation — split the market into groups with meaningfully different needs (behavioral/needs-based beats demographic alone).
Targeting — pick which segment(s) to pursue, based on size, growth, and fit with the company's strengths.
Positioning — define how you want the target segment to perceive you relative to alternatives, in one clear, differentiated statement.
when_to_use: Use it for "who should we target" or "how should we position this product" questions - almost always the right starting structure for a branding/launch case.
when_not_to_use: Do not use it as a substitute for a GTM plan - STP tells you who and how you want to be perceived, not the channels/budget/timeline to get there.
pitfalls: Segmenting on demographics alone when behavior/needs-based segments would be sharper (two 28-year-olds can have completely different needs).
A positioning statement that could apply to any competitor - it should name a specific, defensible point of difference.
